title: Pacem in Terris (1963)
hook: a pope writes on rights and peace, and addresses the letter to all people of good will
tomorrow: Signs of the times (Gaudium et Spes)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Quadragesimo Anno: Pius the Eleventh's letter, and the idea that what a small group can do well, a bigger one shouldn't swallow. Your line was from the ground up. Did you let a group decide something? Day one thousand three hundred two.

Night, a field outside Bethlehem, and shepherds hear the sky fill with voices. In Luke's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, the song goes: "Glory to God in the highest; and on earth peace to men of good will." Peace on earth. In Latin, pacem in terris. Those words became the name of a letter from Pope John the Twenty-third. And the letter took something else from the angels' song: its audience. It is addressed to bishops and clergy and the faithful, and then, at the end of the greeting, to all men of good will. Anyone could open it and find their name on the envelope. Today's word is that letter.
screen: `ON EARTH PEACE.` → `PACEM IN TERRIS.` → `TO ALL PEOPLE OF GOOD WILL.`

segments.voice: First, the list. Pacem in Terris sets out rights that belong to a person simply for being a person. The right to life and to the things that keep it going: food, clothing, shelter, rest, medical care. The right to learn. The right to worship God as conscience directs. The right to work, to meet with others, to move from place to place, to take part in public life. The letter doesn't present these as favors a government hands out. They come with being human. Second, the other half of every right, the pairing this block met with Cain, now set down in the letter itself. It is careful here: a right in one person brings a duty, in that same person and in everyone around them. My right to life is my duty to look after it, and your duty to respect it. A society that shouts only about rights, the letter suggests, is building with one hand. Third, what peace stands on. John the Twenty-third names four things: truth, justice, charity and freedom. Peace, in this letter, isn't just the quiet after the guns stop. It's a building, and those are its four walls. Take one away, and the roof sags. Which brings it down to an ordinary week. A treaty table is a long way from an ordinary week. But truth told at work, a fair deal, care for a neighbor, and room for others to choose are the same four walls, built smaller. The angels sang peace to people of good will. The letter takes good will as something people can practice, one wall at a time.
screen: `RIGHTS THAT COME WITH BEING HUMAN.` · `EVERY RIGHT HAS A DUTY BESIDE IT.` · `TRUTH, JUSTICE, CHARITY, FREEDOM.` · then, large: `ON EARTH PEACE TO MEN OF GOOD WILL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for peace talks. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one table where people are trying to talk instead of fight. It might be between two countries in the news. It might be a city council, or a family that has stopped speaking. Picture the people sitting there, tired, wary, still at the table. Give each of the four walls one breath: truth, justice, charity, freedom. If you pray, you can hold them before God with the angels' line: on earth peace to men of good will. If you don't, simply keep that table in mind and wish it well. The bell holds the time.

Pacem in Terris. Peace on earth: rights, duties and four walls, for all people of good will. This week's road: the poor first, work has dignity, one family, our common home, a just wage, from the ground up, and now peace on earth. Today's word.
Your line: peace on earth. Pick one of the four walls today, truth, justice, charity or freedom, and lay one brick of it somewhere small. Day one thousand three hundred two.

howItsDone: Catholics often pray for peace at Mass in the prayers of the faithful, and Pacem in Terris is still read and taught in Catholic schools, parishes and peace groups as a charter of human rights and duties.
